title: The first crossword
hook: The first crossword was shaped like a diamond and called a word-cross.
peek: On 21 December 1913, the New York World printed a new puzzle by Arthur Wynne. It was diamond-shaped, had no black squares, and was called a word-cross. Within weeks, reportedly through a typesetting slip, its name had changed for good.
lede: Arthur Wynne, a journalist born in Liverpool, edited the Fun section of the New York World. For the Christmas edition of 1913 he needed something new, and drew a diamond of interlocking boxes with numbered clues. He called it a Word-Cross. Readers loved it, and it became a weekly feature long before most other newspapers carried a crossword.

bullets.text: Wynne's puzzle had a hollow diamond centre and no black squares. He filled the word FUN in at the top as a start, and the clues were listed by the numbers of the first and last squares of each answer.
A few weeks after the first puzzle, the title was printed as Cross-Word, and the new name stuck. Over time the hyphen dropped away, leaving the word crossword.

In 1924 the new publishers Simon and Schuster released the first book of crossword puzzles, with a pencil attached. It sold strongly, and a nationwide craze followed in which crosswords appeared everywhere.
Later puzzle editors added black squares and, in America, rules such as rotational symmetry. These conventions grew from readers' tastes rather than from Wynne's first design.
